Speed Limit Review - 
update 
The Department of Transport carried out a Review of 
Speed Limits nationally and this has resulted in changes 
to the default speed limits for roads in Ireland. These 
changes were signed into law in April 2024.   The 
changes to the legislation will reduce the default speed 
limits on some road categories including:  
• 
60km/hr on Rural Local Roads (reduction 
from 80km/hr) 
• 
80km/hr on National Secondary Roads 
(currently 100km/hr) 
• 
30km/hr in Urban Areas (currently 
predominantly 50km/hr). 
 
The default speed limit commenced nationally on 7 
February 2025 and all Rural Local Roads in Tipperary 
now have a 60kmh speed limit. There was no 
requirement to revoke any element of our existing 
Special Speed Limit Byelaws. The stretches of Local 
Roads within urban areas (USLZ) were not part of this 
Phase One. 
It is proposed by the National 
Group that implementation of the 
speed limits will be done in phases:  
• 
Phase 1 - Rural Local 
Roads 
• 
Phase 2 - National 
Secondary Roads and 
Urban Areas  
• 
Phase 3 - Other Special 
Circumstances, such as 
schools.   
Maps are being prepared for Phase 
2.   Notification of the 
commencement of the Special 
Speed Limit process issued in late 
January to relevant stakeholders. 
The time line for progression of 
further phases is now delayed 
nationally.

Ballina/Killaloe By Pass, Shannon Bridge Crossing (Brian Boru Bridge) and 
R494 Improvement Scheme 
 
Official Opening 
 
On 22nd May 2025, the Minister for Transport, 
Darragh O’Brien TD officially opened the 
Ballina/Killaloe 
Bypass, 
Shannon 
Bridge 
Crossing and R494 Improvement Scheme.   This 
road project is a transformative 6.2km 
development which includes the first new 
vehicular bridge across the Shannon in more 
than three decades.  
The project is located in the vicinity of the twin 
towns of Killaloe, Co Clare and Ballina, Co 
Tipperary, on opposite sides of the River 
Shannon.  It provides a western bypass of 
Killaloe, the first new vehicular bridge crossing 
over the Shannon since 1991, and an upgrade of 
the existing R494 regional road from Ballina to 
Birdhill, Co. Tipperary.  
The bridge, jointly named as the Brian Boru 
Bridge, was a complex engineering feat for those 
involved in the project that took 2.5 years to 
complete. The initial overall cost estimate for the 
scheme was approximately €88 million. 
The scheme will greatly improve the quality of 
life for residents of both towns. The alternative 
route will take through traffic and HGVs out of 
both town centres, thereby significantly reducing 
congestion, protecting both heritage areas, and 
providing a much-needed boost to the local 
economy and the region’s tourism sector. 
The project was listed in the National 
Development Plan and comprises: 
• 
2km of new single carriageway bypass 
around the town of Killaloe which 
connects the R463 to the north of the 
town with the Brian Boru Bridge section 
and R494 to the south of the town; 
• 
a new single carriageway bridge jointly 
named in honour of Brian Boru, 
crossing over the River Shannon 
approximately 1km south of the existing 
Killaloe Bridge and connecting the 
Killaloe Bypass with the R494; 
• 
the 
upgrade 
and 
realignment 
of 
approximately 3.3km of the existing 
R494 from its junction with the R496 
and Brian Boru Bridge south of Ballina, 
as far as the junction with the R445 
(previously known as N7) north of 
Birdhill, and the M7 link road; 
• 
the provision of dedicated, high quality 
new cycling and pedestrian facilities 
along the approximately 6.2km length of 
road development; 
• 
the new Brian Boru bridge over the 
Shannon at Ballina-Killaloe is the first 
new vehicular bridge across the river 
since the opening of Shannon Way 
Bridge in 1991. 
Speaking at the official opening, Minister 
O’Brien said: “I am delighted to officially open 
this 
transformative 
road 
project, 
which 
strengthens 
the 
connection 
between 
communities in Clare and Tipperary.

With approximately €88m million in funding 
allocated by my Department, this represents a 
significant Government investment in regional 
infrastructure and underscores our ongoing 
commitment to investing in and modernising 
Ireland’s road network. “Road safety remains a 
key priority in all our infrastructure projects. The 
completion of the project will significantly 
enhance safety and efficiency for all road users. 
The inclusion of dedicated pedestrian and 
cycling facilities not only improves safety but 
also encourages more sustainable, active travel 
along this vital corridor.” 
 
 
 
 
 
Cathaoirleach of Tipperary County Council Cllr 
Declan Burgess said: “The completion of the 
Brian Boru bridge is a historic day for the people 
of Ballina and Killaloe. There can be no stronger 
symbol of the connection between the twin 
towns than Brian Boru, celebrated equally on 
both sides of the river. The finished scheme will 
remove traffic from the towns and allow them 
to fulfil their potential for both the existing 
residents and the many tourists that will be 
attracted to the area. This is a proud day for all 
of the people of Clare and Tipperary, and the 
twin towns can look forward to a bright future 
together.”

The Derelict Sites Act requires the owner of a building or land to ensure that they do not become or 
continue to be derelict. The Act defines a derelict site as being any land which detracts, or is likely to 
detract, to a material degree from the amenity, character or appearance of land in the 
neighbourhood.  
 
 
At the start of 2025 the derelict sites register contained 84 properties and the owners of these 
properties were issued with a letter reminding them of their obligations under the Act to carry out 
works to render the buildings non-derelict. To date we have removed 4 of these properties from the 
register as the works have been carried out. In April the register has been updated now contains 81 
properties. These property owners will be receiving a derelict site levy letter which is due to be issued 
in July 2025.   
 
We have issued a further 22 properties with letters advising them of works needed to render the 
property non-derelict.  
 
The team have commenced two CPO processes and aim to increase the level of interaction with 
property owners to increase the awareness of the focus on vacancy and dereliction countywide.  
 
URDF Call 3 
URDF Call 3 seeks to tackle long term vacant and derelict buildings and sites across URDF towns and 
cities primarily in order to accelerate the provision of residential development and regenerate town 
centres.  An allocation of €5m has been approved for Tipperary County Council under this Call. 
There are 77 properties on the list divided between the URDF designated towns of Clonmel, Nenagh 
and Thurles and we have received approval to begin adding more properties to this list. Of these 77 
properties 40 are in the process of being removed from the list as there are works underway or they 
have now been deemed to be not vacant or derelict. The team are engaging with the other 37 
property owners to determine the best course of action to bring these properties back into use.  
We are in the process of adding a further 22 properties to the list.
